definition.text: The ability of people, institutions, ecosystems and other organisms to adjust to potential harm, seize opportunities or cope with consequences.

facts.text: In climate risk, adaptive capacity sits alongside hazard, exposure and vulnerability as a key component of risk.
It works as a stock of resources and assets from which adaptations can be drawn as future conditions require.
In social systems it rests on institutions that learn, flexible decision-making and power structures responsive to all stakeholders.
The ODI's local adaptive capacity framework names five features: assets, institutions and entitlements, knowledge, innovation, and flexible forward-looking governance.
A stable, prosperous economy helps, and wealthier nations are generally better prepared for climate impacts.
Barriers to adaptation can be overcome, whereas limits cannot; lack of land to relocate to is a common external barrier.
For species, it depends on phenotypic plasticity, dispersal ability and genetic diversity.

title: Climate change adaptation

definition.text: The process of adjusting to current and expected effects of climate change, to reduce harm and take advantage of opportunities.

facts.text: It usually goes alongside mitigation, which limits warming by cutting greenhouse gas emissions.
Examples include seawalls, new insurance schemes, changing crop planting times and installing green roofs.
Adaptation can be reactive, responding to impacts, or proactive, preparing for future change.
It matters most in developing countries, which are most vulnerable to climate change.
More than 70% of countries have adaptation plans, but actual implementation is limited and uneven.
Knowledge gaps, behavioural resistance and market failures slow adaptation and call for policy.
In the early 1990s adaptation was seen as a distraction from mitigation; it gained attention in 2009–2010 after the Copenhagen Summit.
Politicians are rewarded for short-term change, so long-term adaptation is hard to carry through.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

title: Types of adaptation options
article: Climate change adaptation#Options by type of action

definition.text: The four kinds of adaptation action: infrastructural, institutional, behavioural and nature-based.

facts.text: Built-environment options protect against flooding, sea level rise and extreme heat.
Institutional responses include zoning rules, building codes, insurance schemes and coordination.
Behavioural options include farmers changing planting times or switching crops and livestock.
Nature-based solutions work with ecosystems to benefit both people and biodiversity.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

title: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

definition.text: The cost of adapting to climate change, and the shortfall between that cost and the money available, known as the adaptation gap.

facts.text: Costs rise sharply with more warming; globally they likely run to tens or hundreds of billions of dollars a year for decades.
The IPCC puts adaptation costs at $15 to 411 billion per year to 2030, with most estimates above $100 billion.
The gap is widening because most tracked climate finance goes to mitigation.
UNEP's 2023 report put the adaptation finance gap at $194 billion to $366 billion a year.
Developing countries' needs, $215 to $387 billion a year, are 10–18 times current international public adaptation finance.
In many specific settings, adaptation investment costs less than the damage it avoids, though global estimates are very uncertain.

title: International adaptation finance

definition.text: Money from richer countries and international funds that helps developing countries adapt to climate change.

facts.text: UNFCCC funds include the Special Climate Change Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund and the Adaptation Fund.
In 2009 rich nations pledged $100 billion a year by 2020 for mitigation and adaptation; by December 2020 it had not been fully delivered.
The Green Climate Fund was created in 2010 as one channel for this finance.
Adaptation received only 21% of public climate finance provided in 2020.
Multilateral development banks gave over €19 billion for adaptation in 2021.
In 2022 nations agreed to set up a loss and damage fund for harms beyond what adaptation can handle.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

title: Additionality in adaptation finance

definition.text: The principle that adaptation money should be extra to existing development aid rather than redirected from it.

facts.text: Four main definitions exist, from finance additional to the Millennium Development Goals to climate finance unconnected to aid budgets.
Critics say it encourages business as usual because it ignores future climate risks.
Denmark raised adaptation aid from 0.09% to 0.12% of GDP between 2010 and 2020 by taking it from other aid.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

title: Maladaptation

definition.text: An adaptation action that ends up increasing vulnerability to climate change or reducing the ability to adapt sustainably later.

facts.text: The IPCC introduced the term in 2001 and notes it is usually an unintended consequence.
Adjusting to short-term variability can be maladaptive for long-term trends, as with irrigation expansion in Egypt's Western Sinai.
Air conditioning powered by carbon-intensive electricity adds to the emissions causing the problem.
Seawalls can waterlog fields and reduce soil fertility.
Community-driven bottom-up approaches generally carry lower risk of maladaptation than top-down technical fixes.
The IPCC first introduced the term in 2001.

The IPCC describes it as actions that may raise climate-related risk, including through higher greenhouse gas emissions, shifted vulnerability, more inequitable outcomes or reduced welfare; it is usually unintended.
Adapting to short-term climate swings can cause maladaptation to longer-term trends, as with irrigation expanded into Egypt's Western Sinai desert despite projected drying.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap
notes: The seed page 'Maladaptation' is about evolutionary biology; the course sense lives in Climate change adaptation#Maladaptation, used as article. The biological sense is one fact only.

title: Limits to adaptation

definition.text: The points beyond which adaptation can no longer protect people or ecosystems from climate risks.

facts.text: The IPCC's 2022 report distinguishes soft limits, where options exist but are not yet usable, from hard limits.
Some systems in Australia, small islands, the Americas, Africa and Europe have already hit soft limits.
At 1.5 °C, glacier-dependent regions and small islands reach hard limits; at 2 °C many staple crops hit soft limits.
As risks grow, incremental adjustments become insufficient and larger, costlier transformational adaptation is needed.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

title: Barriers to private adaptation investment
article: Climate change adaptation#Incentivizing private investment in adaptation

definition.text: The reasons private investors find adaptation harder to fund than mitigation, chiefly the lack of a clear income stream.

facts.text: Adaptation often serves non-market sectors or public goods that benefit many, so few projects attract private money.
Costs come now while benefits come later, and investors prefer short-term returns.
Uncertainty about future impacts and benefits leaves investors short of information.
Innovation is increasing the potential for private finance to help close the adaptation gap.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

title: Adaptation–mitigation synergies and trade-offs

definition.text: The ways actions to adapt to climate change and actions to limit it can reinforce or work against each other.

facts.text: Public transport is a synergy: lower emissions per kilometre and easier evacuation in disasters.
Compact cities cut transport and building emissions but can worsen the urban heat island.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

title: Climate risk factors
article: Climate change adaptation#Reduce risk factors: vulnerability and exposure

definition.text: The three interacting ingredients of climate risk: the hazard, the exposure of people and assets, and their vulnerability.

facts.text: Exposure is the presence of people, livelihoods, ecosystems and assets in places that could be harmed.
Exposure falls with retreat from floodplains and better early warning and evacuation.
Vulnerability, the IPCC's propensity to be adversely affected, includes sensitivity and lack of capacity to cope.
Insurance, livelihood diversification, social protection and sturdier infrastructure reduce vulnerability.
Protecting mangroves, which dampen storm energy, is ecosystem-based adaptation that cuts vulnerability.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

title: Climate services

definition.text: Systems that deliver usable climate information to people and organisations to support adaptation, mitigation and risk decisions.

facts.text: They help users foresee and manage hazards of a changing climate.
They are demand-driven, designed with users through co-design, rather than supply-driven research products.

distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

title: Climate resilience

definition.text: How well people or ecosystems can cope with, and bounce back from, climate hazards such as floods and droughts.

facts.text: The IPCC defines it as the capacity of social, economic and ecosystems to cope with a hazardous event, trend or disturbance, including the ability to reorganise and learn.
Its definition is heavily debated because the idea crosses many disciplines.
One framework splits it into adaptive, anticipatory and absorptive capacity.
Most resilience work so far maintains existing systems, such as seawalls protecting a coastal community, an incremental rather than transformational approach.
Adaptation is any adjustment to climate impacts, while resilience is a more systematic way of absorbing change and reorganising.
Long-lived infrastructure needs risk-based engineering and economic analysis to design for resilience under uncertain projections.

contested_note: The definition of resilience is contested in both concept and practice.

title: Climate resilient development

definition.text: Development that pursues adaptation, mitigation and sustainable development together, using their synergies and reducing trade-offs.

facts.text: It has become a new, if contested, paradigm for sustainable development, especially in the water sector.
Governments on every continent are adopting policies for climate-resilient economies, pushed by the Paris Agreement and the SDGs.

contested_note: Sources describe the paradigm itself as contested.

definition.text: Tools and indicators for tracking the climate resilience of households, communities or nations to guide spending on resilience.

facts.text: It helps locate vulnerability hotspots and judge whether interventions work.
Resilience has no single observable metric and includes intangibles like social capital, so toolkits rely on long lists of proxy indicators.
Common objective measures include FAO's RIMA and the Livelihoods Change Over Time index.

title: Climate risk insurance

definition.text: Insurance designed to cover the financial risks of climate change, especially extreme weather.

facts.text: It gives quick money after disasters for relief and rebuilding, and is seen as an important adaptation measure.
Because weather disasters hit whole regions at once and trigger many claims together, it must be sold at a large, diversified scale.
High premiums in risky areas could discourage people from settling there.
Critics say it puts the cost on communities that emitted least, and start-up and data costs are high for low-income countries.
The InsuResilience Global Partnership, launched at COP23, supports such schemes.
It is often seen as a way to improve the climate resilience of poor and developing communities.
It provides money after a disaster for relief and rebuilding, and helps prepare to reduce future vulnerability.
Insurance pools risks, but because climate risks are partly correlated, pooling works less well for them.

contested_note: Critics argue it shifts costs onto low-emitting communities, while supporters see it as a safety net.

title: Loss and damage

definition.text: The harms from climate change that mitigation and adaptation fail to prevent, and the question of how to deal with them.

facts.text: Loss means irreversible harm, such as extinction or islands lost to sea; damage means harm that can be repaired or compensated.
Economic losses affect traded goods and services; non-economic losses, like lost family members or cultures, involve things not traded in markets.
It covers both sudden disasters such as cyclones and slow-onset change such as sea level rise.
Small island and least developed countries have long sought liability and compensation, which developed countries resist.
In 1991 small island states proposed an insurance pool funded by countries' shares of emissions and income; it was rejected.
A 2026 study estimated US CO2 emissions from 1990 to 2020 caused $10.2 trillion in cumulative damages by 2020.
The IPCC found residual risks beyond adaptation will rise with further warming.

contested_note: How governments should respond, especially on liability and compensation, has been disputed since the UNFCCC adopted the term.

title: Warsaw International Mechanism
article: Loss and damage (climate change)#Warsaw International Mechanism for Loss and Damage

definition.text: The UN body created in 2013 to address loss and damage in highly vulnerable countries through research and dialogue.

facts.text: It recognises that loss and damage can go beyond what adaptation can reduce.
It makes no provision for liability or compensation, and the Paris Agreement says it gives no basis for either.
Developed countries, particularly the United States, insisted on the no-liability clause.

title: Loss and Damage Fund
article: Loss and damage (climate change)#Loss and Damage Fund

definition.text: A climate finance fund agreed at COP27 in Egypt in 2022 to support communities where adaptation is inadequate or comes too late.

facts.text: It was agreed after years of negotiation.
Before the June 2023 Paris finance summit, over 100 economists proposed an extreme wealth tax to fund loss and damage; it was not adopted.
It was agreed after three decades of negotiation on loss and damage and was seen by many as a major breakthrough.
It operates as a financial mechanism of the Paris Agreement.

title: Disaster risk reduction

definition.text: Actions that make disasters less likely and less damaging, by preventing new risk, reducing existing risk and managing what remains.

facts.text: Disaster risk is the potential loss of life, injury or damaged assets, arising from hazard, vulnerability and exposure together.
It aims to make communities more resilient and less vulnerable.
Its scope is much broader than conventional emergency management; disaster risk management is its practical implementation.
Experts often see climate change adaptation as one of many processes within DRR.
Since the mid-1970s the field has shifted from response and recovery toward understanding causes and reducing risk beforehand.
Women and girls are disproportionately harmed: after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, 77% of deaths in North Aceh were female.
It aims to make communities stronger and better prepared, that is, more resilient and less vulnerable.
It is also called DRR or disaster risk management.

distinct_from: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction

title: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction
article: Disaster risk reduction#Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction

definition.text: The international framework adopted on March 18, 2015, setting seven targets for reducing disaster risk to 2030.

facts.text: It aims to cut disaster deaths, people affected, economic loss and damage to infrastructure.
Other targets increase access to warning systems, aid to developing countries and national DRR strategies.
Countries with national DRR strategies rose from 55 to 123 by 2022.

title: Economics of disaster risk reduction
article: Disaster risk reduction#Financing needs and finance flows

definition.text: The costs of disasters and the case for spending on prevention rather than only on response and recovery.

facts.text: Climate-related disasters have cost over US$330 billion a year on average over 2015–2021, likely an underestimate.
Every dollar spent on risk reduction saves between $5 and $10 in disaster losses.
Yet around 90% of international DRR funding goes to response and recovery, and only about 0.5% of development aid goes to pre-disaster risk reduction.
For many countries less than 1% of the national budget is available for DRR.
New instruments include risk disclosure rules, resilience bonds and green bonds.

distinct_from: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction

definition.text: The state of being open to harm; for hazards, the features of a community, system or asset that make it susceptible to damage.

facts.text: In disasters, vulnerability ties people's relationship with their environment to social forces, institutions and cultural values.
Risk is proportional to vulnerability: the more vulnerable a community, the more risk it faces.
Indicators cover external shocks and stresses as well as internal inability to cope.
Climate vulnerability is generally a bigger problem in low-income than in high-income countries.

definition.text: The inability of people, organisations and societies to withstand harm from multiple stresses such as social exclusion and natural hazards.

facts.text: It arises partly from social interactions, institutions and cultural values.
Marital status, employment and income affect individual vulnerability.
Understanding catastrophe requires looking at people's assets and entitlements, not just the severity of shocks.

definition.text: How strongly people or ecosystems are likely to be harmed by climate change; formally, their propensity to be adversely affected.

facts.text: It includes capacity to cope and adapt, and is one component of climate risk.
Earlier IPCC reports made vulnerability a function of exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity; the Fifth report moved exposure to be a separate element of risk.
About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people were estimated in 2021 to live in highly vulnerable contexts.
People with low incomes, Indigenous peoples, women, children and the elderly tend to be more vulnerable.
Developing countries were judged more vulnerable, partly because adaptation costs are high relative to their GDP.
It can be reduced by adaptation, by tackling poverty, inequality and conflict, and by mitigation that makes impacts less severe.

definition.text: The main split between biophysical vulnerability, the effects of physical hazards, and social vulnerability, shaped by political, economic and social structures.

facts.text: Early studies focused on biophysical vulnerability, drawing on natural hazards research.
Social vulnerability is a people-centred view of why some are harmed more, driven by poverty, poor governance and conflict.
Place-based vulnerability is highest where sea level rise and changes in ecosystem services such as food access strike.

definition.text: Tools that measure climate vulnerability, from global indices to local models and participatory methods, to guide responses.

facts.text: Global indices include the ND-GAIN Country Index, the INFORM Risk Index and the WorldRiskIndex.
Composite indices usually average a set of standardised indicators into a score.
Vulnerability curves link levels of a hazard, such as extreme heat or sea level rise, to the damage caused.

definition.text: The branch of anthropology that studies how human cultures adapt to and shape their environments.

facts.text: It emerged in the 1960s from Julian Steward's cultural ecology.
Roy Rappaport's work with the Maring of Papua New Guinea examined ritual in the relationship between culture and nature.
Long-term traditional ecological knowledge can inform adaptation strategies and community monitoring.
Critics said it assumed static equilibrium and oversimplified systems, prompting a shift toward political ecology.

definition.text: An international fund under the Kyoto Protocol that pays for projects helping developing countries adapt to climate change.

facts.text: It was established in 2001 at COP7 in Marrakech and officially launched in 2007.
Its original funding was a 2% share of credits issued for CDM projects; as carbon prices fell, donations from rich countries became more important.
Its direct access mechanism lets accredited national and regional bodies in developing countries receive funds directly.
By 2024 it had committed over 1 billion US dollars since 2010 and reports over 43 million beneficiaries.

conflicts.text: The Adaptation Fund resulted from negotiations at COP15 and COP16 in 2009 and 2010.
conflicts.note: The Adaptation Fund page says it was established in 2001 and launched in 2007 (de7d48d120da); the CDM page says it was established in 2007 (e13102edd0f0).

definition.text: Strategies for reducing climate risk that draw on adaptation, disaster management and sustainable development.

facts.text: It is a general approach to climate-sensitive decisions that aims to reduce vulnerability.
Tools include early response systems, diversification, flexible resource-allocation rules, insurance, infrastructure design and capacity building.
It also seeks gains, such as farmers using favourable seasonal forecasts to raise yields.

title: Crop insurance

definition.text: Government-subsidised insurance bought by farmers against crop losses from disasters such as hail, drought and floods, or against lost revenue.

facts.text: Governments stepped in because markets failed to give farmers tools to manage production risk.
Hail insurance is offered privately because hail is a narrow, local peril; multi-peril cover is vulnerable to large-scale events.
In the United States the federal government subsidises on average 62 percent of the premium, and about 90% of crop acreage is insured.
India's National Agriculture Insurance Scheme insures whole areas rather than individual farms, paying for yield shortfalls against the past five years.

notes: Dossier text is mostly US and Canadian programme detail; facts kept to the general mechanism.

definition.text: A chain of sensors, detection and communication that spots hazards early and gives people time to prepare and limit harm.

facts.text: A complete system covers risk analysis, monitoring and warning, dissemination and communication, and response capability.
To work, it must involve at-risk communities, raise awareness, spread alerts effectively and keep people prepared.
The UN recommends early warning systems as key to climate adaptation, and runs the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems partnership for high-risk countries.
Interest surged after the Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004.

definition.text: Insurance, mainly for farming, that pays out when an index closely tied to losses, such as rainfall or yield, crosses a set trigger.

facts.text: Assessing actual losses is too costly for smallholders in developing countries, so traditional indemnity insurance is usually not viable.
Paying by index avoids the cost of checking individual claims.
It sidesteps moral hazard because no one can manipulate the weather that triggers payment.
Weather disasters hit many people at once, unlike thefts, which makes them hard to insure conventionally.
Many indices now use satellite imagery.
In developing countries it has so far needed subsidies to be viable, and uptake among smallholders remains low.

definition.text: The mismatch in index insurance between what the index pays and the losses a particular farmer actually suffers.

facts.text: An index covers an area where farmers' experience of rainfall can differ, so some lose crops but get no payout, or vice versa.
Because of basis risk, farmers are reluctant to pay the same premiums as for standard insurance.
Researchers aim to reduce it with new data sources.

definition.text: The rise in average ocean level, which has sped up sharply as human-caused warming expands seawater and melts land ice.

facts.text: Between 1901 and 2018 global average sea level rose 15–25 cm, faster than in at least 3,000 years; the rate reached 4.62 mm per year in 2013–2022.
From 1993 to 2018, melting ice sheets and glaciers caused 44% of the rise and thermal expansion of water 42%.
It lags temperature by decades, so it will keep accelerating to 2050 from warming already caused.
By 2100 it could be 30 cm to 1.0 m above the early 2020s with very deep emission cuts, or up to 1.9 m with high emissions.
Impacts include more storm-surge flooding, coastal erosion, loss of mangroves, saltier irrigation water and damaged ports.
Low-lying Caribbean and Pacific islands face the greatest near-term impact, and many may become uninhabitable this century.
Socially and economically vulnerable communities are often more exposed and have fewer resources to adapt.

definition.text: The ways societies respond to rising seas: retreating, accommodating coastal change, or protecting coasts with hard or soft defences.

facts.text: Cutting emissions can slow sea level rise after 2050 but cannot stop it, so adaptation is inevitable.
Hard adaptation relies on capital-intensive infrastructure such as seawalls; soft adaptation strengthens natural defences like dunes with local, modular means.
Adaptation in 136 large coastal cities could cut annual flood costs from $1 trillion by 2050 to a little over $60 billion, at a cost of $50 billion per year.
Higher-value areas are more likely to be protected, leaving lower-value areas to retreat.
Retreat often costs livelihoods, and displaced people can strain their new communities.
In a 2023 survey of planners, 98% knew the projections but 26% had not yet put them into policy.

definition.text: Insurance against losses from flooding, one of the most widely used forms of climate risk insurance.

facts.text: Rising sea levels, floods and windstorms threaten the affordability of flood-exposed areas.
Critics say the subsidised US programme encouraged building and rebuilding in floodplains and coasts.
Its rules make flood-prone homes more likely to be rented cheaply to low-income, older or infirm people, an example of adverse selection.

definition.text: A flood with a one percent chance of being equalled or exceeded in any year, also called the 100-year flood, used to define floodplains.

facts.text: Flood likelihoods are worked out by statistical analysis of streamflow records.
Urban growth increases runoff, so flood maps based on older data may understate hazards.

title: National Flood Insurance Program

definition.text: A US federal programme created in 1968 to share flood losses through insurance and reduce damage by restricting floodplain building.

facts.text: Communities join by enforcing floodplain rules for new construction in mapped Special Flood Hazard Areas.
Flood insurance became mandatory for property in those areas under a 1973 amendment.
Repetitive-loss properties cost it about $200 million a year, according to a 2003 GAO finding.

notes: Single-country (US) programme; the general lessons are drafted under Flood insurance and Base flood.
